title: Clustering as inference: K-means and soft K-means
bookRef: ITILA ch. 20 (An Example Inference Task: Clustering), ch. 22 (Maximum Likelihood and Clustering)
audience: Adults who finished sessions s01-s13: probability, Bayes' theorem, entropy, the bent coin, model comparison, maximum likelihood with Gaussians, Monte Carlo.
objectives: Run the K-means algorithm by hand: assignment step, then update step.
Explain soft K-means: responsibilities as posterior probabilities of cluster membership.
Connect soft K-means to maximum likelihood for a mixture of Gaussians.
Recognise the failure modes: bad initialisation, choosing K, and the collapsing-Gaussian singularity of maximum likelihood.
keyIdeas: K-means alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest mean; move each mean to the average of its points. The total squared distance never increases.
Soft K-means replaces hard assignments with responsibilities r_k(x) proportional to exp(-beta * distance^2), normalised over clusters; beta is a stiffness (inverse width).
Responsibilities are Bayes' theorem: prior weight of each cluster times the Gaussian likelihood of the point, normalised.
Maximum likelihood for a Gaussian mixture can put one component on a single point with width shrinking to zero: infinite likelihood, useless model.
misconceptions: K-means finds the best clustering (it finds a local optimum that depends on the start).
More clusters always mean a better model (the fit always improves; compare models with the evidence instead, as in session 10).
Hard assignments are certain (points between clusters genuinely belong partly to both).
exercisesNeeded: One K-means update in 1D: given points and two means, compute the new means.
Soft responsibilities for a point between two clusters given beta.
